title.rendered: Blessed Are Those Who Mourn: The Gospel For Today

excerpt.rendered: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.” A morning devotional for anyone carrying grief today.

content.rendered:
The world’s message is simple. Do not cry. Push through. Move on. Get over it. Jesus stood on a hillside in Galilee and said something the world has never quite known what to do with. Blessed are those who mourn.

The Gospel For Today | Saturday, August 29, 2026

Today’s Scripture

“Blessed are those who mourn, For they shall be comforted.”
Matthew 5:4 (NKJV)

Today’s Message

The world’s message about grief is simple and consistent. Do not cry. Push through. Move on. Get over it. Every culture has a slightly different version of the same instruction. Bury the loss quickly. Do not linger in the pain. Do not let the tears be seen. And then Jesus stood on a hillside in Galilee, in front of an audience shaped by exactly that kind of cultural expectation, and said something the world has never quite known what to do with. “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.” Not blessed are those who suppress. Not blessed are those who push through. Blessed are the ones who let themselves feel what is actually there.

Jesus is continuing the beatitudes of the Sermon on the Mount. Yesterday we heard the first. Blessed are the poor in spirit. Today He names the second. The Greek word for “mourn” here is pentheō, the strongest word for grief in the Greek New Testament. It is the word used for weeping over a death. It is not sadness. It is not disappointment. It is the deep, wet-cheeked, shoulder-shaking grief of a heart that has genuinely lost something it loves. Jesus calls that kind of grief, in a Kingdom person, blessed.

The beatitude reaches in multiple directions at once. It applies to the believer grieving over their own sin, the way David grieved in Psalm 51 after Nathan confronted him. It applies to the believer grieving over the brokenness of the world, the way Jeremiah wept over Jerusalem and Jesus wept over the same city centuries later. It applies to the believer grieving over the loss of loved ones, the way Mary and Martha grieved over Lazarus. And it applies to the believer grieving over the wounds of their own life, the ones nobody sees, the ones we have been told to push through. Jesus does not tell any of these mourners to push through. He tells them they are blessed, and He promises them comfort.

The Passion Translation opens up the tenderness of the promise: “What delight comes to you when you wait upon the Lord! For you will find what you long for. The Anointed One will strengthen you as you weep” (Matthew 5:4 TPT). The Amplified Bible Classic Edition adds: “Blessed and enviably happy [with a happiness produced by the experience of God’s favor and especially conditioned by the revelation of His matchless grace] are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted!” (Matthew 5:4 AMPC). Comfort is not the absence of grief. Comfort is the presence of God inside the grief. The Greek word for “comforted” here is parakaleō, the same root as Paraklētos, the name Jesus later uses for the Holy Spirit. The One called alongside. The Comforter.

For Gospelbuzz readers today, this beatitude is one of the most personal in the entire Sermon on the Mount. Wherever you are reading this from, in Lagos or London or Manila or Nairobi or Sao Paulo, if you have been carrying a grief the world has been telling you to bury faster, Jesus is telling you today that the grief is not your enemy. He is not asking you to pretend. He is not asking you to be embarrassed by your tears. He is calling you blessed inside them. And He is promising the personal comfort of the Holy Spirit, called alongside you, staying with you as long as the grief lasts, until He has walked you through to the other side. Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.

Prayer

Father, I acknowledge that Jesus called the mourners blessed. He did not tell me to bury my grief faster or push through my pain in isolation. He called me blessed inside the tears. Today I bring You the grief I have been carrying. The losses. The disappointments. The wounds. The heaviness that has been sitting on my heart. I stop pretending. I let You in. And I trust the promise of Your Son. The Holy Spirit, the Comforter, is called alongside me today. I am not alone in this. In Jesus’ name. Amen.

Declaration

Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. I do not push my grief away today. I bring it into the presence of the Comforter. The Holy Spirit is called alongside me. I am not alone.
